topics.summary: The previous chapters examined individual layers. This chapter follows one small program through the complete path: source text becomes instructions, the executable becomes mappings, instructions access translated memory, and I/O requests cross into the kernel. Each layer contributes a different kind of correctness and a different class of failure. The example computes a byte count and an unsigned 64-bit byte sum from standard input. The sum is intentionally simple and wraps modulo 2^64 ; the count rejects overflow rather than wrapping. Neither result is a cryptographic integrity guarantee. The simple operation makes the surrounding system behavior easy to inspect.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.1 Source Code → Compiler
topics.summary: Source code describes behavior under a language standard. Declarations establish types and interfaces; definitions provide objects and function bodies. The preprocessor handles includes and macros before the compiler’s language analysis. The compiler must reason about the program’s allowed behavior, including integer rules, object lifetime, aliasing, and observable effects. A pointer-and-length interface carries preconditions even when its machine representation is only two integer-like values. Invalid source-level behavior is not repaired by the fact that the target CPU can execute some corresponding instruction sequence. [ R1 , R8 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.2 Compiler → Assembly
topics.summary: The compiler lowers the program into target instructions and chooses registers, branches, addressing modes, and transformations. The source loop need not survive as one literal assembly loop; optimization may unroll or vectorize it while preserving required behavior. The unsigned byte sum permits reassociation under modular arithmetic in ways that a strict floating-point sum might not. Numeric semantics therefore influence available machine implementations. Compare generated assembly only after identifying which transformations the source contract permits. [ R2 , R3 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.3 Assembly → Object Code
topics.summary: The assembler encodes instructions and data into a relocatable object file. Symbols identify definitions and references, while relocation records describe locations that need adjustment when final addresses are determined. An object file is not yet necessarily a runnable executable. A call to checksum_update can refer to a symbol whose final location is unresolved until linking. Debug information and symbol tables help tools explain the relationship between source and machine code without being the code’s runtime semantics themselves.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.4 Object Code → Linker
topics.summary: The linker combines object files and resolves symbols against other objects and libraries. It lays out the resulting program according to the executable format and link options. Missing definitions, incompatible interfaces, and duplicate definitions appear at this boundary. The C declaration and definition must agree. A successful link does not prove that a mismatched manually declared ABI is correct, and linking a library does not prove that its runtime dependencies will be available. Build correctness includes the intended headers, object versions, options, and target architecture. [ R1 , R37 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.5 Executable → Loader
topics.summary: Execution asks the operating system to replace a process image with the executable. The kernel validates and interprets the executable format and establishes the initial execution environment. Dynamically linked programs also involve a runtime linker or loader according to the platform’s format and configuration. main is not normally the very first instruction executed. Startup code establishes language-runtime state before calling it. Understanding this explains why a program can fail before reaching the first source line of main , for example when a required dynamic library cannot be loaded. [ R16 ]

topics.title: 60.10 Program → System Call
topics.summary: The program calls read to obtain input and write to emit its result. Library wrappers marshal arguments into the operating-system ABI and translate return conventions into the documented C interface. This is where an I/O return value becomes a memory-safety boundary. [ R11 , R12 , R46 ]

topics.title: 60.11 System Call → Kernel
topics.summary: The kernel resolves the descriptor, checks the request, and performs or waits for the relevant operation. Standard input may be a regular file, pipe, terminal, or another endpoint, so the same user code can trigger different kernel paths. A blocking read may let another task run, while a read satisfied from available data may return without switching processes. Kernel entry, blocking, and context switching are separate events. Error and short-progress results return responsibility to the program’s control flow.

topics.summary: The public interface states that data designates at least length valid bytes whenever length is nonzero. The function borrows the bytes and retains no pointer. Chapter 60 — From Source Code to Running Program
VERBATIM GRADUATE LECTURE TRANSCRIPT
Charles Dorner

SLIDE 1: Chapter 60 — From Source Code to Running Program

LECTURE NARRATION
The previous chapters examined individual layers. This chapter follows one small program through the complete path: source text becomes instructions, the executable becomes mappings, instructions access translated memory, and I/O requests cross into the kernel. Each layer contributes a different kind of correctness and a different class of failure. The example computes a byte count and an unsigned 64-bit byte sum from standard input. The sum is intentionally simple and wraps modulo 2^64 ; the count rejects overflow rather than wrapping. Neither result is a cryptographic integrity guarantee. The simple operation makes the surrounding system behavior easy to inspect.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, the previous chapters examined individual layers.
